summary: Describes using counter modes of block ciphers such as AES with ESP and AH when many senders protect group traffic. Counter modes assume one sender increments the counter, so group use needs special handling.

plainLanguage.summary: A counter mode cipher uses a ticking counter. If many people in a group all share one counter, they could clash. This explains how to stop that.

questions: how do multiple senders share a counter mode key in ipsec
what is a sender identifier in esp
why must ipsec ivs be unique
subtitle: How many senders can share one IPsec key with counter-mode ciphers without ever repeating an IV.

tldr.problem: Counter-mode ciphers used with ESP and AH are only safe if no key, IV and Salt combination ever protects two different payloads, but group applications have many senders sharing one Security Association.
tldr.mechanism: Each IV is built from a Sender Identifier (SID) in the leftmost bits and a Sender-Specific IV (SSIV) in the rest, and the group key management system hands out a unique SID to each sender.
tldr.outcome: With this partitioning of the IV space, security is equivalent to the single-sender case, as long as the group key manager and the members follow the rules.

facts.label: IV layout
facts.value: SID on the left, SSIV in the remaining bits

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and the Authentication Header (AH) are the security protocols of IPsec. Several counter-based modes have been defined for them, among them AES Counter Mode, Galois/Counter Mode (GCM), CCM and GMAC, plus Camellia and GOST counter modes. They offer advantages over traditional modes of operation.

All of them restrict how they may be used when multiple senders protect traffic with the same key. This document describes how these modes can be used with group key management protocols such as GDOI and GSAKMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some fast ciphers need a never-repeating number for every message. This document explains how a whole group can share one secret and still never repeat a number.

sections.title: The Problem with Shared Keys
sections.content:
Counter-based modes require that, if one key is shared by several encryption engines, those engines coordinate so that every Initialization Vector (IV) used with that key is distinct. In cryptographic terms the IV is a nonce. The rule is stated as: an application must not use the same key, IV and Salt values to protect two different data payloads. This differs from CBC mode, which needs unpredictable IVs.

For point-to-point use, the counter mode transforms build their keying material from IKEv2, which guarantees the condition for a single sender. Some group applications can simply create one IPsec Security Association (SA) per sender. But in Many-to-Many Applications, one SA protects traffic between members of a multiple-sender IP multicast application, and with a large number of senders an SA per sender is unmanageable.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally one person numbers their own tickets. When a whole crowd shares one ticket book, they need a plan so two people never grab the same number.

sections.title: Forming the IV from a Sender Identifier
sections.content:
Each IV is the concatenation of a Sender Identifier (SID) and a Sender-Specific IV (SSIV). The leftmost bits hold the SID and the remaining bits hold the SSIV. The SID MUST be unique for each sender across all senders sharing an SA. The SSIV MUST be unique for each IV a given sender builds for that SA, and may be chosen in any convenient way, for example successive counter values.

The SID length can vary with group policy, but every SID used with one SA MUST have the same length. Implementations MUST support SID lengths of 8, 12 and 16 bits. The SID size is a trade-off: it sets the number of possible senders against the number of packets each sender can send on that SA.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ticket number starts with the sender's own badge number, followed by that sender's private count. Two different badges can never produce the same ticket.

sections.title: Group Key Management Conventions
sections.content:
A Group Key Management System (GKMS), made of one or more Group Controller and Key Server entities, distributes IPsec policy and keys to group members. The RFC RECOMMENDS that the GKMS allocate unique SIDs and distribute them with a protocol such as GDOI or GSAKMP. Sequential allocation is fine if the rules are followed.

  • The GKMS MUST NOT give the same SID to more than one active member for an SA. If unsure which SID a member holds, it MUST allocate a new one. Several distributing entities MUST NOT hand out overlapping sets.
  • If the SIDs run out, the GKMS MUST refuse new members, or it could distribute replacement SAs, possibly with larger SID values.
  • The GKMS SHOULD give each member one SID for all group SAs where it sends, which also makes rekeying simpler.
  • A SID of a departed member MAY be reallocated, but only after the GKMS has deleted and replaced any active AH or ESP SAs the SID was used with.
sections.plainLanguage: A referee gives each child a unique badge number. If the badges run out, no new children can join, and a badge is only reused after the old tickets are thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
By partitioning the possible IV values so that each cryptographic device has exclusive use of a set, the method keeps the algorithms as secure as in the conventional single-sender case, provided the recommendations are followed. The security of the group depends on members behaving correctly: a member using an SID not allocated to it may reduce the security of the system.

A device that keeps keying material across a reboot must also store the SID and SSIV values used with each SA so it never reuses counters. A member that reaches the end of its IV space MUST stop sending on that SA and should re-register with the GCKS. The specification does not address virtual machine rollbacks that may cause nonce reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must stick to their own numbers, and remember them even after a nap. If you run out of numbers, you stop and ask the referee for more.

sections.title: Why the SID Lives in the Explicit IV
sections.content:
The SID could have gone into either the Salt or the explicit IV field. The explicit IV was chosen because it is visible in every packet. With the SID in the Salt, a receiver would have to infer the sender, for example from the IP source address, and that gets harder when ESP is carried over UDP for NAT traversal.

The equal-length requirement for SIDs is not strictly necessary and was added for simplicity. The RFC notes that SIDs could instead be codewords of a prefix-free code, since then no SID is a prefix of another, but this was disallowed in favor of simplicity over generality.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the badge number right on the ticket means the person reading it never has to guess who sent it.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
A group has one SA shared by all senders, using AES-GCM with an 8-bit SID. The first sender to register gets SID 1 and sends IVs 0x0100000000000001, 0x0100000000000002 and so on, up to 0x01FFFFFFFFFFFFFF. The second sender gets SID 2 and uses 0x0200000000000001 up to 0x02FFFFFFFFFFFFFF.

If the GCKS later distributes a replacement SA, each sender keeps the SID it already has, so the sender with SID 2 again starts at 0x0200000000000001 on the new SA.
sections.plainLanguage: Sender 1 numbers tickets starting with 01, sender 2 with 02. They never overlap, and when a new ticket book arrives they keep their badge numbers.
